einzeiler: Investigating the 1999 Russian apartment bombings and the rise of Vladimir Putin.
kurzfassung: In September 1999, four apartment bombings across Russia killed around 300 people and left the country terrified. The attacks fueled public panic and set the stage for Vladimir Putin's rise to power as prime minister. Decades later, journalists revisit the tragedies and a disputed fifth bomb that points toward a dark conspiracy.
stichpunkte: Four apartment bombings across Russia in September 1999 killed approximately 300 people.
President Boris Yeltsin faced severe economic turmoil, plummeting popularity, and health issues.
The first bombing occurred on September 4 in Buynaksk, followed by blasts in Moscow and Volgodonsk.
Public fear was immediately directed at Chechen militants amid an ongoing brutal conflict.
Vladimir Putin emerged as prime minister during the crisis, promising a forceful response.
A discovered fifth unexploded bomb linked the trail to the FSB, sparking enduring conspiracy theories.
Investigating the bombings has proven dangerous, with multiple journalists losing their lives.

beschreibung:
Four bombs. Twelve days. Hundreds dead. What really happened in Russia in September 1999?
Helena speaks to BBC foreign correspondent Andrew Harding to revisit a story that has haunted him for decades. Following the collapse of the Soviet Union, Harding takes us inside a world of power struggles, inflation and a country on the brink. Then, in September 1999, just weeks after Vladimir Putin becomes Prime Minister, the apartment bombs begin. Russia is gripped by fear. The question is: who did it?
In Season 1 of The History Bureau, presenter Helena Merriman returns to one of the most contested -- and consequential-- stories in modern Russia. In September 1999, just weeks after Vladimir Putin became Prime Minister, four bombs blew up four apartments buildings across Russia. The bombs exploded in the middle of the night, killing hundreds of people while they slept. In this season, Merriman returns to the story with the reporters who were there on the ground. What did they get right first time around? And, in the chaos and confusion of unfolding events, what did they miss?
